arXiv:1910.08980v1 [quant-ph] 20 Oct 2019

Obstacles to State Preparation and Variational Optimization
from Symmetry Protection

Sergey Bravyi Affiliation: IBM T.J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, NY 10598, USA    Alexander Kliesch Affiliation: Zentrum Mathematik, Technical University of Munich, 85748 Garching, Germany    Robert Koenig Affiliation: Institute for Advanced Study & Zentrum Mathematik, Technical University of Munich, 85748 Garching, Germany    Eugene Tang Affiliation: Institute for Quantum Information and Matter, Caltech, Pasadena, CA 91125
Abstract

Local Hamiltonians with topological quantum order exhibit highly entangled ground states that cannot be prepared by shallow quantum circuits. Here, we show that this property may extend to all low-energy states in the presence of an on-site ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry. This proves a version of the No Low-Energy Trivial States (NLTS) conjecture for a family of local Hamiltonians with symmetry protected topological order. A surprising consequence of this result is that the Goemans-Williamson algorithm outperforms the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for certain instances of MaxCut, at any constant level. We argue that the locality and symmetry of QAOA severely limits its performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose a non-local version of QAOA, and give numerical evidence that it significantly outperforms standard QAOA for frustrated Ising models on random 33-regular graphs.

Classifying topological phases of matter is amongst the main objectives of modern condensed matter physics [1]. Central to this program is the characterization of entanglement structures that can emerge in ground states of many-body systems. Of particular interest are topologically non-trivial ground states [2]. Such states cannot be generated by a constant-depth quantum circuit starting from a product state. Non-trivial states exhibit complex, non-local entanglement properties and are thus expected to have highly non-classical features. Remarkably, certain gapped local Hamiltonians have non-trivial ground states. For example, preparing a ground state of Kitaev’s toric code [3] from a product state requires a circuit depth growing at least polynomially in the system size using using nearest-neighbor gates [4], and logarithmically using non-local gates [5].

Going beyond ground states, a natural next question is whether there are local Hamiltonians with the property that any low-energy state is non-trivial. Formalized by Freedman and Hastings [6], this is known as the No Low-energy Trivial States (NLTS) conjecture. To state it in detail, consider many-body systems composed of nn finite-dimensional subsystems – assumed here to be qubits for simplicity. A local Hamiltonian is a sum of interaction terms acting non-trivially on O⁡(1)O(1) qubits each. We require that each term has operator norm O⁡(1)O(1) and each qubit is involved in O⁡(1)O(1) terms. The interaction terms may be long-range (no geometric locality is needed). It will be assumed that a local Hamiltonian HnH_{n} as above is defined for each n∈ℐn\in{\cal I}, where ℐ{\cal I} is some infinite set of system sizes. A family of local Hamiltonians {Hn}n∈ℐ\{H_{n}\}_{n\in{\cal I}} is said to have the NLTS property if there exists a constant ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and a function f:ℤ+→ℤ+f\,:\,\mathbb{Z}_{+}\to\mathbb{Z}_{+} such that:
(1) HnH_{n} has ground state energy 00 for any n∈ℐn\in{\cal I},
(2) ⟨0n|U†​Hn​U|0n⟩>ϵ​n\langle 0^{n}|U^{\dagger}H_{n}U|0^{n}\rangle>\epsilon n for any depth-dd circuit UU composed of two-qubit gates and for any n≥f⁡(d)n\geq f(d), n∈ℐn\in{\cal I}.
Here the circuit depth dd can be arbitrary. The conjecture is that the NLTS property holds for some family of local Hamiltonians.

The validity of the NLTS conjecture is a necessary condition for the stronger quantum PCP conjecture to hold [7]: the latter posits that there are local Hamiltonians whose ground state energy is QMA-hard to approximate with an extensive error ϵ​n\epsilon n for some constant ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

A proof of the NLTS conjecture is still outstanding. Although many natural families of Hamiltonians provably do not have the NLTS property (see [8] for a comprehensive list), evidence for its validity has been provided by a number of related results. Ref. [6] constructs Hamiltonians satisfying a certain one-sided NLTS property: these have excitations of two kinds (similar to the toric code), and low-energy states with no excitations of the first kind are non-trivial. The construction crucially relies on expander graphs as even the one-sided NLTS property does not hold for similar constructions on regular lattices [6].

Eldar and Harrow [8] construct families of local Hamiltonians (also based on expander graphs) such that any state whose reduced density operators on a constant fraction of sites coincides with that of a ground state is non-trivial. This feature, called the No Low-Error Trivial States (NLETS) property, is clearly related to robustness of entanglement in the ground state with respect to erasure errors [9, 10]. The existence of Hamiltonians with the NLETS property is a necessary condition [8] for the existence of good quantum LDPC codes, another central conjecture in quantum information.

Here we pursue a different approach to the NLTS conjecture by imposing an additional symmetry in the initial state as well as the preparation circuit. This mirrors similar considerations in the classification of topological phases, where the concept of symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases [11] has been extremely fruitful. Indeed, the study of SPT equivalence classes of states, pioneered in [12, 13], has led to a complete classification of 1D phases [11, 14, 15], and also plays an essential role in measurement-based quantum computation [16, 17].

For concreteness, we focus on the simplest case of onsite ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetry. A local Hamiltonian is said to be ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric if all interaction terms commute with X⊗nX^{\otimes n}, where XX is the single-qubit Pauli-XX operator. Likewise, a quantum circuit UU acting on nn qubits is said to be ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric if it obeys

U​X⊗n=X⊗n​U.\displaystyle UX^{\otimes n}=X^{\otimes n}U\ . (1)

We do not impose the symmetry on the individual gates of UU, though this will naturally be the case in many interesting examples, such as the QAOA circuits considered below. Finally, let us say that a state Ψ\Psi of nn qubits is ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric if X⊗n​Ψ=±ΨX^{\otimes n}\Psi=\pm\Psi. Our first result is a proof of the NLTS conjecture in the presence of onsite ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetry:

Theorem 1.

There exist constants ϵ,c>0\epsilon,c>0 and a family of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric local Hamiltonians {Hn}n∈ℐ\{H_{n}\}_{n\in{\cal I}} such that HnH_{n} has ground state energy 00 for any n∈ℐn\in{\cal I} while

⟨φ|U†​Hn​U|φ⟩>ϵ​n\displaystyle\langle\varphi|U^{{\dagger}}H_{n}U|\varphi\rangle>\epsilon n (2)

for any ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric depth-dd circuit UU composed of two-qubit gates, any ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric product state φ\varphi, and any n≥2c​dn\geq 2^{cd}, n∈ℐn\in{\cal I}.

Our starting point to establish Theorem 1 is a fascinating result by Eldar and Harrrow stated as Corollary 43 in [8]. It shows that the output distribution of a shallow quantum circuit cannot assign a non-negligible probability to subsets of bit strings that are separated far apart w.r.t. the Hamming distance. More precisely, define the distribution p⁡(x)=|⟨x|U|φ⟩|2p(x)=|\langle x|U|\varphi\rangle|^{2}, where x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n}. Given a subset S⊆{0,1}nS\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}, let p⁡(S)=∑x∈Sp⁡(x)p(S)=\sum_{x\in S}p(x).

Fact 1 ([8]).

For all subsets S,S′⊆{0,1}nS,S^{\prime}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n} one has

dist⁡(S,S′)≤4​n1/2​23​d/2min⁡{p⁡(S),p⁡(S′)}.\mathrm{dist}(S,S^{\prime})\leq\frac{4n^{1/2}2^{3d/2}}{\min{\{p(S),p(S^{\prime})\}}}. (3)

Here dist⁡(S,S′)\mathrm{dist}(S,S^{\prime}) is the Hamming distance, i.e. the minimum number of bit flips required to get from SS to S′S^{\prime}. We emphasize that Eq. (3) holds for all depth-dd circuits UU and all product states φ\varphi (ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetry is not needed).

Given a bit string xx let x¯\overline{x} be the bit-wise negation of xx. Note that p⁡(x)=p⁡(x¯)p(x)=p(\overline{x}) since U​φU\varphi is ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric. Choose SS and S′S^{\prime} as the sets of all nn-bit strings with the Hamming weight ≤n/3\leq n/3 and ≥2​n/3\geq 2n/3 respectively. Then p⁡(S′)=p⁡(S)p(S^{\prime})=p(S) and dist⁡(S,S′)=n/3\mathrm{dist}(S,S^{\prime})=n/3. Eq. (3) gives

p(S)≤12n−1/223​d/2.p(S)\leq 12n^{-1/2}2^{3d/2}. (4)

Our strategy is to choose the Hamiltonian HnH_{n} such that low-energy states of HnH_{n} are concentrated on bit strings with the Hamming weight close to 00 or nn such that p⁡(S)p(S) is non-negligible. Then Eq. (4) provides a logarithmic lower bound on the depth dd for symmetric low-energy states.

Suppose G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is a graph with nn vertices. The Cheeger constant of GG is defined as

h⁡(G)\displaystyle h(G) =minS⊆V0<|S|≤n/2⁡|∂S||S|,\displaystyle=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq V\\ 0<|S|\leq n/2\end{subarray}}\frac{|\partial S|}{|S|}\ , (5)

where ∂S⊆E\partial S\subseteq E is the subset of edges that have exactly one endpoint in SS. Families of expander graphs are infinite collections of bounded degree graphs {Gn}n∈ℐ\{G_{n}\}_{n\in{\cal I}} whose Cheeger constant is lower bounded by a constant, i.e. h⁡(Gn)≥h>0h(G_{n})\geq h>0 for all n∈ℐn\in{\cal I}. Explicit constructions of degree-33 expanders can be found in [18]. Fix a family of degree-33 expanders {Gn}n∈ℐ\{G_{n}\}_{n\in{\cal I}} and define HnH_{n} as the ferromagnetic Ising model on the graph GnG_{n}, i.e.

Hn=12​∑(u,v)∈E(I−Zu​Zv).H_{n}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(u,v)\in E}(I-Z_{u}Z_{v}). (6)

Here ZuZ_{u} is the Pauli-ZZ applied to a site uu and II is the identity. Clearly, HnH_{n} is ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric, each term in HnH_{n} acts on two qubits and each qubit is involved in three terms. Thus {Hn}n∈ℐ\{H_{n}\}_{n\in{\cal I}} is a family of local Hamiltonians. HnH_{n} has ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric ground states 12​(|0n⟩±|1n⟩)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0^{n}\rangle\pm|1^{n}\rangle) with zero energy. Given a bit string xx, let 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(x)={j∈[n]:xj=1}\mathsf{supp}(x)=\{j\in[n]\,:\,x_{j}=1\} be the support of xx. From Eqs. (5),(6) one gets

where |x||x| is the Hamming weight of xx. Assume Eq. (2) is false. Then p⁡(x)p(x) is a low-energy distribution such that ∑xp⁡(x)​⟨x|Hn|x⟩≤ϵ​n\sum_{x}p(x)\langle x|H_{n}|x\rangle\leq\epsilon n. By Markov’s inequality, p⁡(x)p(x) has a non-negligible weight on low-energy basis states,

p⁡(Slow)≥1/2,Slow={x:⟨x|Hn|x⟩≤2​ϵ​n}.p(S_{\mathrm{low}})\geq 1/2,\qquad S_{\mathrm{low}}=\{x\,:\,\langle x|H_{n}|x\rangle\leq 2\epsilon n\}. (8)

Then Slow⊆S∪S′S_{\mathrm{low}}\subseteq S\cup S^{\prime} and p⁡(Slow)≤p⁡(S)+p⁡(S′)=2​p​(S)p(S_{\mathrm{low}})\leq p(S)+p(S^{\prime})=2p(S). Here the last equality uses the symmetry of p⁡(x)p(x). By Eq. (8), p⁡(S)≥1/4p(S)\geq 1/4. Combining this and Eq. (4) one gets n1/2≤48⋅23​d/2n^{1/2}\leq 48\cdot 2^{3d/2}. We conclude that Eq. (2) holds whenever n>482⋅8dn>48^{2}\cdot 8^{d}. This proves Theorem 1.

The Hamiltonians Eq. (6) are diagonal in the computational basis and have product ground states |0n⟩|0^{n}\rangle and |1n⟩|1^{n}\rangle. The presence of the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetry is therefore essential: the same family of Hamiltonians do not exhibit NLTS without it. In this sense, the NLTS property here behaves similarly to topological order in 1D systems which only exists under symmetry protection [11, 14].

Theorem 1 implies restrictions on the performance of variational quantum algorithms for combinatorial optimization. Recall that the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) [19] seeks to approximate the maximum of a cost function C:{0,1}n→ℝC:\{0,1\}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} by encoding it into a Hamiltonian Hn=∑x∈{0,1}nC⁡(x)​|x⟩​⟨x|H_{n}=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}C(x)|x\rangle\langle x|. It variationally optimizes the expected energy of HnH_{n} over quantum states of the form U(β,γ)|+n⟩U(\beta,\gamma)|+^{n}\rangle, where

U⁡(β,γ)=∏k=1pei​βk​B​ei​γk​Hn,\displaystyle U(\beta,\gamma)=\prod_{k=1}^{p}e^{i\beta_{k}B}e^{i\gamma_{k}H_{n}},

and where B=∑j=1nXjB=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}. The integer p≥1p\geq 1 is called the QAOA level. It controls non-locality of the variational circuit.

A paradigmatic test case for QAOA is the MaxCut problem. Given a graph Gn=(V,E)G_{n}=(V,E) with nn vertices, the corresponding MaxCut Hamiltonian is defined by Eq. (6). The maximum energy of HnH_{n} coincides with the number of edges in the maximum cut of GnG_{n}. Crucially, the QAOA circuit U⁡(β,γ)U(\beta,\gamma) with the Hamiltonian HnH_{n} as well as the initial QAOA state |+n⟩|+^{n}\rangle obey the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetry property. Furthermore, the circuit U⁡(β,γ)U(\beta,\gamma) has depth O⁡(D​p)O(Dp), where DD is the maximum vertex degree of GnG_{n}. Specializing Theorem 1 to bipartite graphs we obtain an upper bound on the approximation ratio achieved by the level-pp QAOA circuits for the MaxCut cost function (see Appendix A for a proof):

Corollary 1.

For every integer D≥3D\geq 3 there exists an infinite family of bipartite DD-regular graphs {Gn}n∈ℐ\{G_{n}\}_{n\in{\cal I}} such that the Hamiltonians HnH_{n} defined in Eq. (6) obey

1|E|⟨+n|U−1HnU|+n⟩≤56+D−13​D\displaystyle\frac{1}{|E|}\langle+^{n}|U^{-1}H_{n}U|+^{n}\rangle\leq\frac{5}{6}+\frac{\sqrt{D-1}}{3D} (9)

for any level-pp QAOA circuit U≡U⁡(β,γ)U\equiv U(\beta,\gamma) as long as p<(1/3​log2​n−4)​D−1p<(1/3\,\log_{2}n-4)D^{-1}.

Note that any bipartite graph with a set of edges EE has maximum cut size |E||E|. In this case, the left-hand side of Eq. (9) coincides with the approximation ratio, i.e., the ratio between the expected value of the MaxCut cost function on the (optimal) level-pp variational state and the maximum cut size. Thus Corollary 1 provides an explicit upper bound on the approximation ratio achieved by level-pp QAOA. Such bounds were previously known only for p=1p=1 [19]. Statement (9) severely limits the performance of QAOA at any constant level pp, rigorously establishing a widely believed conjecture [20]: constant-level QAOA is inferior to the classical Goemans-Williamson algorithm for MaxCut, which achieves an approximation ratio of approximately 0.8780.878 on an arbitrary graph [21]. Indeed, the right-hand side of Eq. (9) is approximately 5/6≈0.8335/6\approx 0.833 for large vertex degree DD.

QAOA circuits U⁡(β,γ)U(\beta,\gamma) possess a form of locality which is stronger than the one assumed in Theorem 1. Indeed, if pp and DD are constants, the unitary U⁡(β,γ)U(\beta,\gamma) can be realized by a constant-depth circuit composed of nearest-neighbor gates, i.e., the circuit is geometrically local.

A natural question is whether more general bounds on the variational energy can be established for states generated by geometrically local ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric circuits. Of particular interest are graphs that lack the expansion property, such as regular lattices, where the arguments used in the proof of Theorem 1 no longer apply. A simple model of this type is the ring of disagrees [19]. It describes the MaxCut problem on the cycle graph ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}.

Quite recently, Ref. [22] proved that the optimal approximation ratio achieved by level-pp QAOA for the ring of disagrees is bounded above by (2​p+1)/(2​p+2)(2p+1)/(2p+2) for all pp and conjectured that this bound is tight. Here we prove a version of this conjecture for arbitrary geometrically local ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric circuits. To quantify the notion of geometric locality, let us say that a unitary UU acting on nn qubits located at vertices of the cycle graph has range RR if the operator U†​Zj​UU^{\dagger}Z_{j}U has support on the interval [j−R,j+R][j-R,j+R] for any qubit jj. For example, the level-pp QAOA circuit associated with the ring of disagrees has range R=pR=p.

Theorem 2.

Let HnH_{n} be the ring of disagrees Hamiltonian,

Hn=12​∑p∈ℤn(I−Zp​Zp+1),H_{n}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}(I-Z_{p}Z_{p+1}),

where nn is even. Let UU be a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric unitary with range R<n/4R<n/4. Then

1n⟨+n|U†HnU|+n⟩≤2​R+1/22​R+1.\frac{1}{n}\langle+^{n}|U^{\dagger}H_{n}U|+^{n}\rangle\leq\frac{2R+1/2}{2R+1}. (10)

This bound is tight whenever nn is a multiple of 2​R+12R+1.

Since one can always round nn to the nearest multiple of 2​R+12R+1, the bound Eq. (10) is tight for all nn up to corrections O⁡(1/n)O(1/n), assuming that R=O⁡(1)R=O(1).

Let us first prove the upper bound Eq. (10). Define X¯=(X​I)⊗n/2\overline{X}=(XI)^{\otimes n/2}. Then

X¯​Hn​X¯+Hn=n​I\overline{X}H_{n}\overline{X}+H_{n}=nI (11)

Let V=X¯​UV=\overline{X}U. Note that VV is a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetric circuit with range RR. Taking the expected value of Eq. (11) on the state U|+n⟩U|+^{n}\rangle, one infers that Eq. (10) holds whenever

1n⟨+n|V†HnV|+n⟩≥1−2​R+1/22​R+1=12​(2​R+1).\frac{1}{n}\langle+^{n}|V^{\dagger}H_{n}V|+^{n}\rangle\geq 1-\frac{2R+1/2}{2R+1}=\frac{1}{2(2R+1)}. (12)

Thus it suffices to prove that Eq. (12) holds for any ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric range-RR circuit VV. For each j,k∈ℤnj,k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n} define

ϵj,k=12⟨+n|V†(I−ZjZk)V|+n⟩.\epsilon_{j,k}=\frac{1}{2}\langle+^{n}|V^{\dagger}(I-Z_{j}Z_{k})V|+^{n}\rangle.

Let dist⁡(j,k)\mathrm{dist}(j,k) be the distance between jj and kk with respect to the cycle graph ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}. We claim that

ϵj,k=1/2ifdist⁡(j,k)>2​R.\epsilon_{j,k}=1/2\quad\mbox{if}\quad\mathrm{dist}(j,k)>2R. (13)

Indeed, ⟨+n|V†ZiV|+n⟩=0\langle+^{n}|V^{\dagger}Z_{i}V|+^{n}\rangle=0 for any qubit ii since V|+n⟩V|+^{n}\rangle and ZiV|+n⟩Z_{i}V|+^{n}\rangle are eigenvectors of X⊗nX^{\otimes n} with eigenvalues 11 and −1-1. Such eigenvectors have to be orthogonal. From dist⁡(j,k)>2​R\mathrm{dist}(j,k)>2R one infers that V†​Zj​VV^{\dagger}Z_{j}V and V†​Zk​VV^{\dagger}Z_{k}V have disjoint support. Thus

⟨+n|V†ZjZkV|+n⟩=⟨+n|(V†ZjV)(V†ZkV)|+n⟩\displaystyle\langle+^{n}|V^{\dagger}Z_{j}Z_{k}V|+^{n}\rangle=\langle+^{n}|(V^{\dagger}Z_{j}V)(V^{\dagger}Z_{k}V)|+^{n}\rangle
=⟨+n|V†ZjV|+n⟩⋅⟨+n|V†ZkV|+n⟩=0.\displaystyle=\langle+^{n}|V^{\dagger}Z_{j}V|+^{n}\rangle\cdot\langle+^{n}|V^{\dagger}Z_{k}V|+^{n}\rangle=0.

This proves Eq. (13). Suppose one prepares the state V|+n⟩V|+^{n}\rangle and measures a pair of qubits j<kj<k in the standard basis. Then ϵj,k\epsilon_{j,k} is the probability that the measured values on qubits jj and kk disagree. By the union bound,

ϵj,k≤∑i=jk−1ϵi,i+1.\epsilon_{j,k}\leq\sum_{i=j}^{k-1}\epsilon_{i,i+1}. (14)

Indeed, if qubits jj and kk disagree, at least one pair of consecutive qubits located in the interval [j,k][j,k] must disagree. Set k=j+2​R+1k=j+2R+1. Then ϵj,k=1/2\epsilon_{j,k}=1/2 by Eq. (13). Take the expected value of Eq. (14) with respect to random uniform j∈ℤnj\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. This gives

12≤2​R+1n∑i∈ℤnϵi,i+1=2​R+1n⟨+n|V†HnV|+n⟩\frac{1}{2}\leq\frac{2R+1}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\epsilon_{i,i+1}=\frac{2R+1}{n}\langle+^{n}|V^{\dagger}H_{n}V|+^{n}\rangle

proving Eq. (12). In Appendix B we construct a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-symmetric range-RR circuit UU such that U|+n⟩U|+^{n}\rangle is a tensor product of GHZ-like states on consecutive segments of 2​R+12R+1 qubits. We show that such circuit saturates the upper bound Eq. (10). This completes the proof of Theorem 2.

Concerns about limitations of QAOA have previously been voiced by Hastings [20] who showed analytically that certain local classical algorithms match the performance of level-11 QAOA for Ising-like cost functions with multi-spin interactions. Hastings also gave numerical evidence for the same phenomenon for MaxCut with p=1p=1, and argued that this should extend to p>1p>1 [20].

Motivated by these limitations, we propose a non-local modification of QAOA which we call the recursive quantum approximate optimization algorithm (RQAOA). To sketch the main ideas behind RQAOA consider an Ising-like Hamiltonian

Hn=∑(p,q)∈EJp,q​Zp​ZqH_{n}=\sum_{(p,q)\in E}J_{p,q}Z_{p}Z_{q} (15)

defined on a graph Gn=(V,E)G_{n}=(V,E) with nn vertices. Here Jp,qJ_{p,q} are arbitrary real coefficients. RQAOA aims to approximate the maximum energy maxz⁡⟨z|Hn|z⟩\max_{z}\langle z|H_{n}|z\rangle, where z∈{1,−1}nz\in\{1,-1\}^{n}. It consists of the following steps.

First, run the standard QAOA to maximize the expected value of HnH_{n} on the state |ψ⟩=U(β,γ)|+n⟩|\psi\rangle=U(\beta,\gamma)|+^{n}\rangle. For every edge (j,k)∈E(j,k)\in E compute Mj,k=⟨ψ∗|Zj​Zk|ψ∗⟩M_{j,k}=\langle\psi^{*}|Z_{j}Z_{k}|\psi^{*}\rangle, where ψ∗\psi^{*} is the optimal variational state.

Next, find a pair of qubits (i,j)∈E(i,j)\in E with the largest magnitude of Mi,jM_{i,j} (breaking ties arbitrarily). The corresponding variables ZiZ_{i} and ZjZ_{j} are correlated if Mi,j>0M_{i,j}>0 and anti-correlated if Mi,j<0M_{i,j}<0. Impose the constraint

Zj=sgn⁡(Mi,j)​ZiZ_{j}=\mathrm{sgn}{(M_{i,j})}Z_{i} (16)

and substitute it into the Hamiltonian HnH_{n} to eliminate the variable ZjZ_{j}. For example, a term Zj​ZkZ_{j}Z_{k} with k∉{i,j}k\notin\{i,j\} gets mapped to sgn⁡(Mi,j)​Zi​Zk\mathrm{sgn}{(M_{i,j})}Z_{i}Z_{k}. The term Ji,j​Zi​ZjJ_{i,j}Z_{i}Z_{j} gets mapped to a constant energy shift Ji,j​sgn​(Mi,j)J_{i,j}\mathrm{sgn}{(M_{i,j})}. All other terms remain unchanged. This yields a new Ising Hamiltonian Hn−1H_{n-1} that depends on n−1n-1 variables. By construction, the maximum energy of Hn−1H_{n-1} coincides with the maximum energy of HnH_{n} over the subset of assignments satisfying the constraint Eq. (16).

Finally, call RQAOA recursively to maximize the expected value of Hn−1H_{n-1}. Each recursion step eliminates one variable from the cost function. The recursion stops when the number of variables reaches some specified threshold value nc≪nn_{c}\ll n. The remaining instance of the problem with ncn_{c} variables is then solved by a purely classical algorithm (for example, by a brute force method). Thus the value of ncn_{c} controls how the workload is distributed between quantum and classical computers. We describe a generalization of RQAOA applicable to Ising-like cost functions with multi-spin interactions in Appendix C.

Imposing a constraint of the form (16) can be viewed as rounding correlations among the variables ZiZ_{i} and ZjZ_{j}. Indeed, the constraint demands that these variables must be perfectly correlated or anti-correlated. This is analogous to rounding fractional solutions obtained by solving linear programming relaxations of combinatorial optimization problems. We note that reducing the size of a problem to the point that it can be solved optimally by brute force is a widely used and effective approach in combinatorial optimization.

We compare the performance of the standard QAOA, RQAOA, and local classical algorithms by considering the Ising Hamiltonians in Eq. (15) with couplings Jp,q=±1J_{p,q}=\pm 1 defined on the cycle graph. In Appendix D we prove:

Theorem 3.

For each integer nn divisible by 66 there is a family of 2n/32^{n/3} Ising Hamiltonians of the form Hn=∑k∈ℤnJk​Zk​Zk+1H_{n}=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}J_{k}Z_{k}Z_{k+1} with Jk∈{1,−1}J_{k}\in\{1,-1\} such that the following holds for all Hamiltonians in the family:
(i) There is a local classical algorithm which achieves the approximation ratio 11.
(ii) Level-pp QAOA achieves an approximation ratio of at most p/(p+1)p/(p+1).
(iii) Level-11 RQAOA achieves the approximation ratio 11.

Our definition of local classical algorithms follows [20]. We also show that the level-11 RQAOA achieves the optimal approximation ratio for any 1D Ising model with coupling coefficients Jk∈{1,−1}J_{k}\in\{1,-1\}.

Finally, we numerically compare level-11 versions of QAOA and RQAOA. We consider Ising-type Hamiltonians Eq. (15) with random couplings Jp,q=±1J_{p,q}=\pm 1 defined on random 33-regular graphs. For each problem instance we compute the optimal approximation ratios achieved by the two algorithms, see Figure 1. The level-11 RQAOA significantly outperforms the standard level-11 QAOA for these problem instances. The details of this simulation and further discussion of RQAOA can be found in Appendix C.4.

Appendix C Recursive QAOA

In this appendix, we outline the Recursive QAOA algorithm (RQAOA) for general cost functions.

C.1 Variable Elimination

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a hypergraph with |V|=n|V|=n vertices. Suppose a variable xv∈{1,−1}x_{v}\in\{1,-1\} is associated with each vertex v∈Vv\in V. Let {1,−1}V={1,−1}n\{1,-1\}^{V}=\{1,-1\}^{n} be the set of all possible variable assignments. Let J:E→ℝJ:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a function which assigns a real weight JeJ_{e} to every hyperedge ee. Given a subset f⊂Vf\subset V and an assignment x∈{1,−1}Vx\in\{1,-1\}^{V}, let us write

x⁡(f)=∏v∈fxv.x(f)=\prod_{v\in f}x_{v}.

Let us agree that x⁡(∅)=1x(\emptyset)=1. We consider the problem of maximizing cost functions of the form

C⁡(x)\displaystyle C(x) =∑e∈EJe​x​(e)\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E}J_{e}x(e)\ (39)

over x∈{1,−1}Vx\in\{1,-1\}^{V}.

Fix some vertex v∈Vv\in V. As a motivation, we first describe how a single variable xvx_{v} can be eliminated when a suitably constrained problem is considered. Namely, suppose that instead of trying to approximate maxx∈{1,−1}V⁡C⁡(x)\max_{x\in\{1,-1\}^{V}}C(x), we restrict to x∈{1,−1}Vx\in\{1,-1\}^{V} satisfying

x⁡(f)\displaystyle x(f) =σ,\displaystyle=\sigma, (40)

where f⊂Vf\subset V is some fixed subset of vertices containing vv, and σ∈{1,−1}\sigma\in\{1,-1\} is a constant. If x∈{1,−1}Vx\in\{1,-1\}^{V} satisfies the constraint (40) then

Je​x​(e)=Je​x​(e)​x​(f)​σ=σ​Je​x​(e△f).J_{e}x(e)=J_{e}x(e)x(f)\sigma=\sigma J_{e}x(e\bigtriangleup f).

Here and below A△BA\bigtriangleup B denotes the symmetric difference of sets AA and BB. We arrive at

over all assignments x∈{1,−1}V′x\in\{1,-1\}^{V^{\prime}} coincides with the maximum of C⁡(x)C(x) over all x∈{1,−1}Vx\in\{1,-1\}^{V} satisfying the constraint Eq. (40). ξ​(x)w\displaystyle\xi(x)_{w} ={σ⋅x⁡(f\{v}) for ​v=wxw otherwise\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\sigma\cdot x(f\backslash\{v\})\qquad&\textrm{ for }v=w\\ x_{w}\qquad&\textrm{ otherwise }\end{cases} (47)

for all w∈Vw\in V.

If a global maximum xx of C⁡(x)C(x) happens to satisfy (40), the new reduced problem yields a solution to the original problem.

C.2 Correlation rounding

To construct an approximation algorithm, we simply impose a constraint of the form (40) by choosing f⊂Vf\subset V, v∈fv\in f and σ∈{1,−1}\sigma\in\{1,-1\} appropriately. To make the latter choice, we use the standard 𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠p\mathsf{QAOA}_{p} algorithm with p=O⁡(1)p=O(1). That is, let us set

HG​(J)=∑e∈EJe​Z​(e) where Z⁡(e)=∏v∈eZv\displaystyle H_{G}(J)=\sum_{e\in E}J_{e}Z(e)\qquad\textrm{ where }\qquad Z(e)=\prod_{v\in e}Z_{v}\ (48)

and write H=HG​(J)H=H_{G}(J). We first use the standard 𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠p​(H)\mathsf{QAOA}_{p}(H) algorithm to find an optimal state

Ψ=ΨHG​(β∗,γ∗)∈(ℂ2)⊗|V|\Psi=\Psi_{H_{G}}(\beta_{*},\gamma_{*})\in(\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes|V|}

maximing the energy of HGH_{G}. The expected value

Me=⟨Ψ|Z⁡(e)|Ψ⟩M_{e}=\langle\Psi|Z(e)|\Psi\rangle

can be efficiently approximated on a quantum computer for any e∈Ee\in E.

Suppose the state Ψ\Psi is measured in the computational basis giving a string x∈{1,−1}Vx\in\{1,-1\}^{V}. Clearly, if |Mf||M_{f}| is close to 11, then the variables {xv}v∈f\{x_{v}\}_{v\in f} satisfy a constraint of the form (40) with high probability with σ=𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇⁡(Mf)∈{1,−1}\sigma=\mathsf{sign}(M_{f})\in\{1,-1\} and any v∈fv\in f. Thus it is natural to choose ff such that |Mf||M_{f}| is maximal. Combined with the procedure for eliminating the corresponding variable xvx_{v} described in Section C.1, we obtain a subroutine for reducing the problem size by one variable. Pseudocode for this routine is given below.

Imposing a constraint of the form (40) can be viewed as rounding correlations among the variables {xw}w∈f\{x_{w}\}_{w\in f}: indeed, the constraint demands that for v∈fv\in f, the variable xvx_{v} and x⁡(f\{v})x(f\backslash\{v\}) must be perfectly correlated or anti-correlated.

C.3 The recursive QAOA (𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA}) algorithm

The recursive QAOA algorithm (𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA}) we propose here proceeds simply by iterating the process of eliminating one variable at a time until the number of variables reaches some specified threshold value nc≪nn_{c}\ll n. The remaining instance of the problem with ncn_{c} variables is solved by a purely classical algorithm (for example, by the brute force method). Thus the value of ncn_{c} controls how the workload is distributed between the quantum and the classical computers. Pseudocode for the 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} algorithm is given in Fig. 2.

C.4 Classical simulability of level-11 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} for Ising models

Suppose JJ is a real symmetric matrix of size nn. Here we consider Ising-like cost functions such that the corresponding Hamiltonian is

H\displaystyle H =∑1≤p<q≤nJp,q​Zp​Zq.\displaystyle=\sum_{1\leq p<q\leq n}J_{p,q}Z_{p}Z_{q}\ . (49)

The mean values of a Pauli operator Zp​ZqZ_{p}Z_{q} on the level-11 QAOA state

|ΨH(β,γ)⟩=ei​β​Bei​γ​H|+n⟩|\Psi_{H}(\beta,\gamma)\rangle=e^{i\beta B}e^{i\gamma H}|+^{n}\rangle

can be computed in time O⁡(n)O(n) using an an explicit analytic formula. Such a formula was derived for the Max-Cut cost function by Wang et al. [26, Theorem 1]. Below we provide a generalization to general Ising Hamiltonians. Since the total number of terms in the cost function is O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}), simulating each step of 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} takes time at most O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}). Assuming that nc=O⁡(1)n_{c}=O(1), the number of steps is roughly nn so that the full simulation cost is O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}). Crucially, the simulation cost of this method does not depend on the depth of the variational circuit. This is important because 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} may potentially increase the depth from O⁡(1)O(1) to O⁡(n)O(n) since it adds many new terms to the cost function.

Fix a pair of qubits 1≤u<v≤n1\leq u<v\leq n. Let c=cos⁡(2​β)c=\cos{(2\beta)} and s=sin⁡(2​β)s=\sin{(2\beta)}. Then

Here we only consider the case γ=1\gamma=1 since γ\gamma can be absorbed into the definition of JJ.

For more general cost functions including interactions among three or more variables, there are two complications: First, unlike in the Ising case, the variable elimination process will typically increase the degree of non-locality of interactions. Second, mean values of Pauli operators on the QAOA state ΨH​(β,γ)\Psi_{H}(\beta,\gamma) lack a simple analytic formula (as far as we know). However, one can approximately compute the mean values using the Monte Carlo method due to Van den Nest [27]. A specialization of this method to simulation of the level-1 QAOA is described in [28]. The Monte Carlo simulator has runtime scaling polynomially with the number of qubits, number of terms in the cost function, and the inverse error tolerance, see [28] for details. This method also requires no restrictions on the depth of the variational circuit.

An important distinction between QAOA and RQAOA lies in the measurement step. QAOA requires few-qubit measurements to estimate the variational energy as well as the final nn-qubit measurement that assigns a value to each individual variable. This last step is what makes QAOA hard to simulate classically and may lead to a quantum advantage [29]. In contrast, RQAOA only needs few-qubit measurements to estimate mean values of individual terms in the cost function. The nn-qubit measurement step is replaced by the correlation rounding that eliminates variables one by one. One may ask whether the lack of multi-qubit measurements also precludes a quantum advantage. Indeed, in the special case of level-1 variational circuits and the Ising-like cost function RQAOA can be efficiently simulated classically, see above. However, level-pp RQAOA with p>1p>1 as well as level-1 RQAOA with more general cost functions are not known to be classically simulable in polynomial time, leaving room for a quantum advantage.

Appendix D Comparison of QAOA, RQAOA, and Classical Algorithms

D.1 QAOA versus Classical Local Algorithms

In this section, we discuss another limitation of QAOA which results from its locality and the covariance condition discussed in Lemma A.2: we compare QAOA to a certain very simple classical local algorithm (see Lemma D.1 below). We show that there is an exponential number of problem instances for which the classical local algorithm outperforms QAOA.

Let us briefly sketch the notion of a local classical algorithm. We envision that the tuple (Je)e∈E(J_{e})_{e\in E} is given as input. Here we are interested in algorithms which are local with respect to the underlying graph GG. For r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} and v∈Vv\in V, define

Er​(v)=⋃ℓ=1r⋃(e1,…,eℓ) path with v∈e1{e1,…,eℓ}\displaystyle E_{r}(v)=\bigcup_{\ell=1}^{r}\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{\ell})\\ \textrm{ path with $v\in e_{1}$}\end{subarray}}\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{\ell}\} (64)

to be the set of edges that belong to a path starting at vv of length bounded by rr. Consider a classical algorithm 𝒜{\cal A} which on input {Je}e∈E\{J_{e}\}_{e\in E} outputs x=(x1,…,xn)∈{0,1}nx=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n}. We say that 𝒜{\cal A} is rr-local if there is a family of functions {gv:ℝEr​(v)→{0,1}}v∈V\{g_{v}:\mathbb{R}^{E_{r}(v)}\rightarrow\{0,1\}\}_{v\in V} such that the following holds for every problem instance (Je)e∈E∈ℝE(J_{e})_{e\in E}\in\mathbb{R}^{E}: We have

xv\displaystyle x_{v} =gv​({Je}e∈Er​(v)) for every ​v∈V.\displaystyle=g_{v}\left(\{J_{e}\}_{e\in E_{r}(v)}\right)\qquad\textrm{ for every }v\in V\ . (65)

In other words, in an rr-local classical algorithm, every output bit xvx_{v} only depends on edge weights JeJ_{e} belonging to paths of length bounded by rr starting at vv. We note that this definition can easily be generalized to the probabilistic case (e.g., by including local random bits). For the purposes of this section, deterministic functions turn out to be sufficient.

The (choice of) family {gv}v∈V\{g_{v}\}_{v\in V} can be considered as a set of variational parameters for the classical algorithm. To keep the number of variational parameters constant, we consider vertex-transitive graphs GG. Fix v∗∈Vv_{*}\in V. For every v∈Vv\in V, fix an automorphism πv\pi_{v} of GG such that πv​(v∗)=v\pi_{v}(v_{*})=v. Then the sets Er​(v)E_{r}(v) for different v∈Vv\in V can be identified via Er​(v)=πv​(Er​(v∗))E_{r}(v)=\pi_{v}(E_{r}(v^{*})). We say that an rr-local classical algorithm is uniform if (after this identification) gv≡gg_{v}\equiv g for all v∈Vv\in V, i.e., if there is a single function g:ℝEr​(v∗)→{0,1}g:\mathbb{R}^{E_{r}(v_{*})}\rightarrow\{0,1\} specifying the behavior of the algorithm. To obtain general-purpose algorithms (applicable to any instance), the function g:ℝEr​(v∗)→{0,1}g:\mathbb{R}^{E_{r}(v_{*})}\rightarrow\{0,1\} should be chosen adapatively (i.e., potentially depending on the instance). The definition of local classical algorithm sketched here includes e.g., the algorithms considered in Ref. [20], though it is slightly more general as the local functions can be arbitrary.

Let n=6​rn=6r be a multiple of 66. Consider nn-qubit Hamiltonians (cf. (19)) of the form

H⁡(J)=∑k∈ℤnJk​Zk​Zk+1 where J=(J0,…,Jn−1)∈{1,−1}n.H(J)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}J_{k}Z_{k}Z_{k+1}\qquad\textrm{ where }\qquad J=(J_{0},\ldots,J_{n-1})\in\{1,-1\}^{n}\ . (66)

To define locality and uniformity for the cycle graph ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}, let πv​(w)=v+w(modn)\pi_{v}(w)=v+w\pmod{n} be chosen as translation modulo nn for v∈ℤnv\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. We show the following:

Lemma D.1.

There is a subset 𝒮⊂{1,−1}n\mathcal{S}\subset\{1,-1\}^{n} of 2n/32^{n/3} problem instances such that the following holds:

  1. (i)

    𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠p​(H⁡(J))≤p/(p+1){\mathsf{QAOA}_{p}(H(J))}\leq p/(p+1) for every p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and every J∈𝒮J\in\mathcal{S}.

  2. (ii)

    There is a 11-local uniform classical algorithm such that for every J∈𝒮J\in\mathcal{S}, the algorithm outputs x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} such that ⟨x|H⁡(J)|x⟩=1\langle x|H(J)|x\rangle=1.

  3. (iii)

    Level-11 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} achieves the approximation ratio 11.

For every s=(s0,…,s2​r−1)∈{0,1}2​rs=(s_{0},\ldots,s_{2r-1})\in\{0,1\}^{2r} define J=J⁡(s)∈{1,−1}nJ=J(s)\in\{1,-1\}^{n} by

for all a=0,1,…,2​r−1a=0,1,\ldots,2r-1. We claim that the set 𝒮={J⁡(s)|s∈{0,1}2​r}\mathcal{S}=\{J(s)\ |\ s\in\{0,1\}^{2r}\} has the required properties. Consider an instance H⁡(J⁡(s))H(J(s)) with s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}. Define

X¯​(s)\displaystyle\overline{X}(s) =∏a=02​r−1X3​a+1.\displaystyle=\prod_{a=0}^{2r-1}X_{3a+1}\ . (68)

Then H⁡(J⁡(s))H(J(s)) is related to Hℤn=∑j∈ℤnZj​Zj+1H_{\mathbb{Z}_{n}}=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}Z_{j}Z_{j+1} by the gauge transformation

H⁡(J⁡(s))\displaystyle H(J(s)) =X¯​(s)​Hℤn​X¯​(s)−1.\displaystyle=\overline{X}(s)H_{\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\overline{X}(s)^{-1}\ . (69)

Since the QAOA algorithm is invariant under such gauge transformation (see Lemma A.2), we obtain

𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠p​(H⁡(J⁡(s)))=𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠p​(Hℤn)≤pp+1\displaystyle{\mathsf{QAOA}_{p}(H(J(s)))}={\mathsf{QAOA}_{p}(H_{\mathbb{Z}_{n}})}\leq\frac{p}{p+1}\ (70)

where we use the bound

𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠p​(HℤnMaxCut)≤2​p+12​p+2,\displaystyle{\mathsf{QAOA}_{p}(H_{\mathbb{Z}_{n}}^{\mathrm{MaxCut}})}\leq\frac{2p+1}{2p+2}, (71)

proven in [22] for even nn, in combination with Lemma A.2. This shows (i).

For the proof of (ii), consider the classical algorithm 𝒜{\cal A} which on input J=(J0,…,Jn−1)J=(J_{0},\ldots,J_{n-1}) outputs

xv\displaystyle x_{v} =g⁡(Jv−1,Jv) for every ​v∈ℤn,\displaystyle=g(J_{v-1},J_{v})\qquad\textrm{ for every }v\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\ , (72)

where

g⁡(J,J′)\displaystyle g(J,J^{\prime}) ={1 if ​(J,J′)=(−1,−1)0 otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1\qquad&\textrm{ if }(J,J^{\prime})=(-1,-1)\\ 0&\textrm{ otherwise}\ .\end{cases} (73)

Clearly, the algorithm 𝒜{\cal A} is uniform and 11-local, and it is easy to check that the output satisfies ⟨x|H⁡(J)|x⟩=1\langle x|H(J)|x\rangle=1.

The proof of (iii) is given as a part of Lemma D.2. ∎

D.2 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} on the Ising ring

Here we prove that level-11 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} achieves approximation ratio 11 on the ring of disagrees, in sharp contrast to (arbitrary) level-pp QAOA (see Lemma D.1(i)). More generally, level-11 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} produces x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} which maximizes the cost function (that is, achieves approximation ratio 11) for any 1​D1D Ising model where the coupling coefficients are either +1+1 or −1-1.

Lemma D.2.

Consider a cost function of the form

Cn​(x)\displaystyle C_{n}(x) =∑k∈ℤnJk​xk​xk+1 for ​x∈{1,−1}n,\displaystyle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}J_{k}x_{k}x_{k+1}\qquad\textrm{ for }x\in\{1,-1\}^{n}\ , (74)

where Jk∈{1,−1}J_{k}\in\{1,-1\} for all k∈ℤnk\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. Then the level-11 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} produces x∗∈{1,−1}nx^{*}\in\{1,-1\}^{n} such that Cn​(x∗)=maxx∈{1,−1}n⁡Cn​(x)C_{n}(x^{*})=\max_{x\in\{1,-1\}^{n}}C_{n}(x).

It would be interesting to see additional, more general families of examples where approximation ratios achieved by 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} can be computed or lower bounded analytically.

Proof.

Let

H\displaystyle H =∑k∈ℤnJk​Zk​Zk+1.\displaystyle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}J_{k}Z_{k}Z_{k+1}\ . (75)

Observe first that ⟨ΨH​(β,γ)|Zi​Zj|ΨH​(β,γ)⟩=0\langle\Psi_{H}(\beta,\gamma)|Z_{i}Z_{j}|\Psi_{H}(\beta,\gamma)\rangle=0 if |i−j|>2|i-j|>2 since in this case the operators U−1​Zi​UU^{-1}Z_{i}U and U−1​Zj​UU^{-1}Z_{j}U have disjoint support. Lemma C.1 shows that a 𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠1\mathsf{QAOA}_{1}-state ΨH​(β,γ)\Psi_{H}(\beta,\gamma) has expectation values

⟨ΨH​(β,γ)|Zi​Zj|ΨH​(β,γ)⟩\displaystyle\langle\Psi_{H}(\beta,\gamma)|Z_{i}Z_{j}|\Psi_{H}(\beta,\gamma)\rangle ={12​Ji​sin⁡(4​β)​sin⁡(4​γ) if ​j=i+114​Ji​Ji+1​sin2⁡(2​β)​sin2⁡(4​γ) if ​j=i+20 otherwise\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}J_{i}\sin(4\beta)\sin(4\gamma)\qquad&\textrm{ if }j=i+1\\ \frac{1}{4}J_{i}J_{i+1}\sin^{2}(2\beta)\sin^{2}(4\gamma)&\textrm{ if }j=i+2\\ 0&\textrm{ otherwise}\end{cases} (76)

when Jk∈{1,−1}J_{k}\in\{1,-1\} for every k∈ℤnk\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. Thus

|⟨Ψ⁡(β,γ)|Zi​Zi+2|Ψ⁡(β,γ)⟩|≤1/4 for all ​(β,γ).\displaystyle|\langle\Psi(\beta,\gamma)|Z_{i}Z_{i+2}|\Psi(\beta,\gamma)\rangle|\leq 1/4\qquad\textrm{ for all }(\beta,\gamma)\ . (77)

Assume (β∗,γ∗)(\beta^{*},\gamma^{*}) are such that (β∗,γ∗)=arg​max(β,γ)⁡⟨ΨH​(β∗,γ∗)|H|ΨH​(β∗,γ∗)⟩(\beta^{*},\gamma^{*})=\argmax_{(\beta,\gamma)}\langle\Psi_{H}(\beta^{*},\gamma^{*})|H|\Psi_{H}(\beta^{*},\gamma^{*})\rangle. Then we can infer from (76) that

⟨Ψ⁡(β∗,γ∗)|Zi​Zi+1|Ψ⁡(β∗,γ∗)⟩=Ji/2.\displaystyle\langle\Psi(\beta^{*},\gamma^{*})|Z_{i}Z_{i+1}|\Psi(\beta^{*},\gamma^{*})\rangle=J_{i}/2\ . (78)

Combined with (77) and (76) we conclude that

arg​max(i,j):i<j|⟨ΨH(β∗,γ∗)|ZiZj|ΨH(β∗,γ∗)⟩|=(i∗,i∗+1)\displaystyle\argmax_{(i,j):i<j}|\langle\Psi_{H}(\beta^{*},\gamma^{*})|Z_{i}Z_{j}|\Psi_{H}(\beta^{*},\gamma^{*})\rangle|=(i^{*},i^{*}+1) (79)

for some i∗∈ℤni^{*}\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}. Without loss of generality, assume that i∗=n−2i^{*}=n-2. Then, according to (79), the 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} algorithm eliminates the variable xn−1x_{n-1} (i.e., v=n−1v=n-1, f={n−2,n−1}f=\{n-2,n-1\}). By (78), this is achieved by imposing the constraint

xn−1=xn−2​Jn−2\displaystyle x_{n-1}=x_{n-2}J_{n-2} (80)

i.e., σ=Jn−2\sigma=J_{n-2}. The resulting reduced graph G′=(V′,E′)G^{\prime}=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime}) has vertex set V′=V\{n−1}=ℤn−1V^{\prime}=V\backslash\{n-1\}=\mathbb{Z}_{n-1} and edges

E′\displaystyle E^{\prime} ={{i,i+1}|i∈ℤn\{n−2}}∪{{n−2,0}}\displaystyle=\left\{\{i,i+1\}\ |\ i\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}\backslash\{n-2\}\right\}\cup\{\{n-2,0\}\} (81)
={{i,i+1}|i∈ℤn−2},\displaystyle=\left\{\{i,i+1\}\ |\ i\in\mathbb{Z}_{n-2}\right\}\ , (82)

and it is easy to check that the new cost function takes the form

C′​(x)\displaystyle C^{\prime}(x) =1+∑k∈ℤn−1Jk′​xk​xk+1\displaystyle=1+\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n-1}}J_{k}^{\prime}x_{k}x_{k+1} (83)

with

Ji′\displaystyle J^{\prime}_{i} ={Ji when ​i≠n−2Jn−2​Jn−1 when ​i=n−2\displaystyle=\begin{cases}J_{i}\qquad&\textrm{ when }i\neq n-2\\ J_{n-2}J_{n-1}&\textrm{ when }i=n-2\end{cases} (84)

We note that the transformation (84) preserves the parity of the couplings in the sense that

∏k∈ℤnJk\displaystyle\prod_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}J_{k} =∏k∈ℤn−1Jk′.\displaystyle=\prod_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n-1}}J_{k}^{\prime}\ . (85)

Inductively, the 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} thus eliminates variables xn−1,xn−2,…,xncx_{n-1},x_{n-2},\ldots,x_{n_{c}} while imposing the constraints (cf. (80))

xn−1\displaystyle x_{n-1} =xn−2​Jn−2\displaystyle=x_{n-2}J_{n-2} (86)
xn−2\displaystyle x_{n-2} =xn−3​Jn−3′\displaystyle=x_{n-3}J^{\prime}_{n-3} (87)
⋮\displaystyle\ \ \vdots (88)

arriving at the cost function Cnc​(x)C_{n_{c}}(x) associated with an Ising chain of length ncn_{c} having couplings belonging to {1,−1}\{1,-1\}. Because of (85) and because (75) is frustrated if and only if ∏k∈ℤnJk=−1\prod_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}J_{k}=-1, we conclude that any maximum x∗∈{1,−1}ncx^{*}\in\{1,-1\}^{n_{c}} of Cnc​(x)C_{n_{c}}(x) satisfies

Cnc​(x∗)\displaystyle C_{n_{c}}(x^{*}) ={nc+1 if ​∏k∈ℤnJk=1nc−2 otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}n_{c}+1\qquad&\textrm{ if }\prod_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}J_{k}=1\\ n_{c}-2\qquad&\textrm{ otherwise}\ .\end{cases} (89)

Because the cost function acquires a constant energy shift in every variable elimination step (cf. (83)), the output x=ξ⁡(x∗)x=\xi(x^{*}) of the 𝖱𝖰𝖠𝖮𝖠\mathsf{RQAOA} algorithm satisfies

C⁡(x)\displaystyle C(x) =n−nc+Cnc​(x∗)={n+1 if ​∏k∈ℤnJk=1n−2 otherwise.\displaystyle=n-n_{c}+C_{n_{c}}(x^{*})=\begin{cases}n+1\qquad&\textrm{ if }\prod_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}}J_{k}=1\\ n-2\qquad&\textrm{ otherwise}\ .\end{cases} (90)

This implies the claim. ∎
